## TITLE

Helmet Turn Signal System With Handlebar Switches

## CROSS-REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATIONS

Not applicable.

## BACKGROUND

The present disclosure relates to signaling devices for riders of bicycles, scooters, and motorcycles. Riders often signal turns with hand gestures, which can be hard for drivers to see at night and which take a hand off the handlebar.

## SUMMARY

In some embodiments, a method of signaling from a helmet includes receiving, by a controller of the helmet, a first signal from a first switch mounted on a handlebar of a vehicle, and in response activating a first light mounted on a rear portion of the helmet. A second signal from a second switch activates a second light. In some embodiments, a system includes the helmet, the lights, the switches, and the controller. In some embodiments, a non-transitory computer-readable medium stores instructions that cause a processor to perform these operations.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION

FIG. 1 shows a system 100 for signaling turns from a helmet 102 worn by a rider of a vehicle 132, such as a bicycle, a scooter, or a motorcycle. The helmet 102 has a rear portion 104 that faces traffic behind the rider. A first light 106 and a second light 108 are mounted on the rear portion 104. In some embodiments, the first light 106 is on the left side of the rear portion 104 and the second light 108 is on the right side. Each light may include one or more light-emitting diodes. Alternatively, each light may include an incandescent bulb or an electroluminescent strip.

A controller 110 is disposed within the helmet 102. The controller 110 includes a processor 112 and a memory 114. The memory 114 is a non-transitory computer-readable medium that stores instructions. When the processor 112 executes the instructions, the instructions cause the processor 112 to perform the operations described below. In other embodiments, the controller 110 is mounted on an outer surface of the helmet 102 or in a separate housing clipped to a strap of the helmet 102.

A first switch 122 and a second switch 124 are mounted on a handlebar 130 of the vehicle 132. The rider presses the first switch 122 to signal a left turn and the second switch 124 to signal a right turn. A wireless transmitter 126 is coupled to the first switch 122 and the second switch 124. A wireless receiver 118 is coupled to the controller 110. The wireless transmitter 126 sends a first signal when the first switch 122 is pressed and a second signal when the second switch 124 is pressed. The first signal and the second signal travel over a wireless link 140 between the handlebar 130 and the helmet 102. In some embodiments, the wireless link 140 is a short-range radio link, for example a link in the 2.4 GHz band. In other embodiments, the switches are wired to a handlebar unit that relays the signals.

An accelerometer 116 is disposed in the helmet 102 and is coupled to the controller 110. The accelerometer 116 measures acceleration of the helmet 102. When the accelerometer 116 detects a deceleration that exceeds a threshold stored in the memory 114, the controller 110 activates the first light 106 and the second light 108 simultaneously as a brake light. The threshold may be set by the rider or at the factory.

FIG. 2 shows a method of signaling from the helmet 102. At step 202, the controller 110 receives the first signal from the first switch 122. At step 204, in response to receiving the first signal, the controller 110 activates the first light 106. At step 206, the controller 110 deactivates the first light 106 after a predetermined period following activation of the first light 106. In some embodiments, the predetermined period is between 5 seconds and 30 seconds. At step 208, the controller 110 receives the second signal from the second switch 124 and, at step 210, activates the second light 108. At step 212, when the accelerometer 116 detects the deceleration, the controller 110 activates both lights.

FIG. 3 shows the rear portion 104 of the helmet 102 with the first light 106 and the second light 108. In some embodiments, the lights extend in a strip across the rear portion 104. In other embodiments, the lights are arranged as arrows pointing left and right.

The embodiments described above are examples. Features of one embodiment may be combined with features of another embodiment, and the order of the steps of the method of FIG. 2 may be changed.

## ABSTRACT

A helmet signaling system includes a helmet with a first light and a second light mounted on a rear portion of the helmet, a first switch and a second switch mounted on a handlebar of a vehicle, and a controller in the helmet. The controller receives a first signal from the first switch over a wireless link and activates the first light, and receives a second signal from the second switch and activates the second light. An accelerometer in the helmet detects a deceleration, and the controller activates both lights when the deceleration exceeds a threshold. The lights may turn off after a predetermined period.
